subject: computer-science

moments.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
moments.body: Dijkstra, then 26, designs his shortest-path algorithm in roughly 20 minutes while having coffee with his fiancee in an Amsterdam cafe. He needed a problem demonstrable to non-specialists to show the power of the new ARMAC computer. He chose the shortest route between two Dutch cities.
moments.takeaway: One of the most-used algorithms in routing, networking and AI search was devised in twenty minutes without paper or pencil — and not published for three years because Dijkstra thought it too trivial.

moments.title: 'Go To Statement Considered Harmful'
moments.body: Dijkstra's letter to Communications of the ACM (titled by editor Niklaus Wirth) argues that goto-based control flow makes programs hard to reason about. The letter triggers the structured programming movement and shapes language design (Pascal, Modula, C).

quote.text: The quality of programmers is a decreasing function of the density of go to statements in the programs they produce.

moments.takeaway: A 1968 polemic by a single computer scientist reshaped how programmers wrote code for decades.

now.title: Algorithms today
now.body: Dijkstra's algorithm runs every time your phone calculates a route. Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, IP routing protocols (OSPF, IS-IS), network packet routing — all variations. The structured programming movement gave us if/while/for and the elimination of goto from most modern languages.
now.open_questions: Does Dijkstra's elegance bias us against messy but effective heuristics? Modern routing combines exact algorithms with learned heuristics (A*, contraction hierarchies).

reflection: Dijkstra wrote his papers by hand and gave them numbers (EWD1 through EWD1318). The 'EWD' archive is still hosted at UT Austin where he taught from 1984. He believed computer science had been corrupted by IBM marketing.
